preview: Rushikesh Chavan shares his detailed BNY internship interview experience consisting of an online assessment and two rigorous rounds covering OOPs, DSA, DBMS, and system design.
content:
Rushikesh chavan  BNY internship interview experience : 
OA: We were given four questions [1 easy, 2 medium, and 1 hard], out 
of which I solved 3 completely [easy  - medium - medium] and partially 
solved the hard one. 
 
First Round: 
The interview panel was assigned in the morning itself. I was waiting 
for my turn, but I wasn't called for a long time. Later, my panel was 
changed, and I became the last one to give the first interview. 
The interview began around 4:15 PM. I greeted the interviewer by his 
name with a warm smile. He asked me to sit and then asked me to 
give an introduction. I had a typical intro format in my mind [I will 
send that separately]. I started the intro, and after the projects part, 
he interrupted me and said, "That's fine, we’ll move ahead." 
Later, he started with the OOPs part. He asked me about the pillars. 
The entire interview felt like a rapid-fire round. Whenever I was 
explaining something, he would pick a word from my sentence and 
instantly ask a follow-up question. 
So while I was talking about inheritance, he interrupted again and 
asked: 
What are classes? 
What is a real-life example of a class? 
What is a real-life example of inheritance?
After answering these, I continued with the rest of the pillars, and 
when I reached polymorphism, he asked me to write a code example 
of polymorphism on paper. I had explained inheritance using the 
example of cars, so I asked him whether I should continue with the car 
class or use another example, to which he replied, "Use the 
BankAccount as the Parent class." 
After writing the code, he verified it and was satisfied with the answer. 
This covered the OOPs section. 
Later, he asked if I had done DSA, to which I replied, "Yes, although it's 
not in my coursework, I love solving challenging problems and 
optimizing solutions, so I actively solve DSA problems and participate 
in contests." 
He then asked me about sorting algorithms, to which I replied with 
the types, time complexities, and the algorithm. He asked me to write 
the code for quicksort on paper. While I was writing, he was doing 
something on his laptop. After I showed him the code, he said there 
was a bug and asked me to recheck. I couldn't find any mistake, so I 
said I wasn't able to spot it and asked if I should dry run it. He said yes, 
so I explained the code to him along with a dry run, and he was 
satisfied. 
[I knew there was no mistake in the code since I had practiced it 
multiple times before the interview.] 
Later, he asked me for an algorithm to reverse an array. I asked 
whether I should start with the brute force approach, to which he 
replied, "Just state the most optimal one." I explained the two-pointer 
solution along with its time and space complexity. This completed the 
DSA part. 
Then he asked me if I had studied DBMS, to which I replied, "Yes, it's 
not in my coursework, but I have studied it to a good level." I was 
pretty confident about it.
He asked me almost every important topic in DBMS. He started with 
the CAP theorem, ACID properties with real-life examples, indexing 
and its need, SQL vs NoSQL and when to use which, partitioning, and 
sharding. 
I noticed a constant smile on his face while I was explaining, so it gave 
me more confidence. 
Later, he asked if I had any questions for him. I asked him two 
questions: 
1) In the PPT, we were told that a team is working on a project 
which includes around 40+ technologies. So to work in that 
team, how many years of experience would I require in BNY? 
2) I have done C++ to a decent level, and now I am feeling 
interested in learning Java and Spring Boot, so at this point 
should I start learning it? What's your take on this? 
He answered these questions, and then he said we were done with 
the interview, to which I said, "Thank you for this opportunity, and I 
am looking forward to working with the organization." 
The interview lasted for around 35–40 minutes [can't remember the 
exact time]. 
 
[My feelings after the first round] 
I never expected that I could answer so smoothly. I was pretty 
confident about my performance and was also sure that I would get 
called for the second round.
Second Round 
Later around 5:30 PM, I was informed that my second round was 
scheduled at 6:00 PM, but it kept getting delayed and finally started 
around 6:40 PM. It was a quick 20-minute round. 
He took my resume and asked me what part I had worked on in the 
first project mentioned. I replied that it was a solo project. He then 
asked me about its working and the use of Redis. I asked him if I could 
use pen and paper, and I explained it to him with diagrams. 
He then asked a follow-up question, saying that with this approach the 
Redis memory might get exhausted after some time. I agreed and 
replied that we can use algorithms like LRU and LFU caching. 
He also asked me about the need for a load balancer and deploying it 
on AWS, to which I replied that I wanted to learn system design 
through practical application. He seemed impressed and gave me a 
compliment: 
"I have interviewed a lot of candidates from premier institutes, 
including IITs, and I have never seen someone from an ECE background 
doing such projects." 
That boosted my confidence to the next level. 
He later asked about the Finance / Equity Research section that I had 
mentioned in my resume, and I gave the prepared explanation. 
Then he asked about the co-curricular activities section from my 
resume, and again I gave the prepared explanation.
After that, he asked about my CGPA. I replied that it is 7.68. He then 
asked why it is comparatively low, to which I explained that I am more 
interested in the software side, and right from the first year I was clear 
that I wanted to work in software for the rest of my life. So I focused 
more on coding instead of studying my core syllabus. 
I also mentioned that we have a few coding subjects like Python and 
C++, where I have scored AA/AB, and that my CGPA graph is 
increasing, with my recent SGPA being 8. 
He seemed pretty satisfied with the answer. 
Later, he asked if I had any questions. I asked him the same question 
from the first round: 
In the PPT, we were told that a team is working on a project 
which includes around 40+ technologies. So to work in that 
team, how many years of experience would I require in BNY? 
He replied that it depends from person to person. Mostly, after getting 
a full-time offer, employees lose their spark and their performance 
reduces, which flattens their learning curve. 
Now here the interesting part begins. I told him how I have the hunger 
for learning and how excited I am to work in that team under his 
guidance. Somehow, the conversation shifted in a different direction, 
and he asked me what is more important in life money or the striving 
nature of human. We had a deep discussion on that topic. 
Later, he said we were done with the interview, and I said, 
"Thank you for this opportunity, and I am looking forward to working 
with the organization." 
 
That's all about both my rounds.  
 
Final result : Selected.
Intro : 
 
Good evening, my name is Rushikesh Chavan, currently studying 
Electronics and Telecommunication at VJTI, Mumbai. 
 
For the past 2 years, I have been exploring the domain of software, 
starting with C++ and DSA in the same language. Later, I moved to 
web development and built a few projects around it, of which the URL 
shortener is quite close to my heart. I have used Redis for caching and 
have deployed two Node.js servers on Railway and one load balancer 
on AWS. 
 
I have also built a group project called Collaborative Learning 
Platform, where we integrated unique features like Strict Mode, 
Dynamic Attendance, and a Collaborative Code Editor. Along with Web 
Development and DSA, I also have strong proficiency in core CS 
fundamentals. 
 
Apart from coding and academics, I am the kind of person who loves 
to participate in multiple events. I have participated as a volunteer, as 
a mentor, and also as a team leader. I am also interested in finance, 
and travelling to hill stations is one of my hobbies. 
 
Thats from my side. And i am looking forward for an interesting 
conversation ahead
